short: Julian's invasion of Persia reached Ctesiphon but killed him in retreat and reversed his gains.
full:
In March 363, the emperor Julian led some 65,000 men down the Euphrates into Sasanian territory, aiming to depose King Shapur II and install a Roman client. The campaign reached the Persian capital Ctesiphon and won a battle outside its walls, but Julian judged the fortified city too strong to besiege and, having burned his own supply fleet, began a difficult retreat north along the Tigris under constant harassment.

On 26 June 363, near Samarra, Julian was fatally wounded in a rearguard skirmish, dying without a named heir; officers hastily elevated the officer Jovian in his place. Jovian negotiated a humiliating peace, ceding territory in Mesopotamia and the fortress of Nisibis that Diocletian had won decades earlier. Julian's death also ended his attempt to revive traditional Roman paganism, leaving Christianity's position in the empire uncontested by an emperor again.
